display_name: Lafage Tessellae Old Vines, Côtes du Roussillon
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "From schist and gneiss slopes across the Roussillon, Tessellae Old Vines builds a dense, dark red with distinct mineral pressure. This cuvée exists to prove that high-volume production can still express site specificity without losing drinkability.",
  "wine_summary": "Operating at a scale few quality producers attempt, Jean-Michel Lafage bottles hundreds of thousands of cases while maintaining farming standards that respect the dry Mediterranean climate. The Tessellae label serves as the entry point to his portfolio, yet the old vine designation signals access to deeper root systems capable of surviving the region's brutal tramontane winds. Roussillon heat concentrates sugars quickly, but the old vines moderate vigor, resulting in a wine that balances ripe fruit weight with structural integrity.",
  "terroir_expression": "Black schist and gneiss dominate the best sites here, storing heat during the day and releasing it at night to ensure full phenolic ripeness even in cooler vintages. These metamorphic rocks fracture easily, forcing roots to dig deep for water, which stresses the vine and reduces yield naturally. The resulting wine carries a dark mineral edge rather than just sweet fruit, distinguishing it from blends grown on alluvial clay near the riverbeds.",
  "vinification_summary": "To preserve primary fruit character, fermentation happens in concrete vats rather than new oak, allowing oxygen exchange through the porous walls. Lafage avoids heavy extraction techniques, opting for a shorter maceration period to keep tannins supple instead of grippy. This approach utilizes partial carbonic maceration elements to enhance freshness, ensuring the wine remains vibrant despite the high alcohol potential of the region.",
  "food_pairing": "Lamb shoulder braised with anchovies works because the salt cuts the ripe fruit while the fat matches the wine's body. Nashville hot chicken finds relief in the wine's glycerol texture and low overt tannin. Grilled sardines with romesco complement the schist-driven smokiness in the finish. Mushroom risotto aligns earthy notes with the old vine depth without overwhelming the palate. Beef cheek tacos stand up to the alcohol warmth while the acid cleanses the fat.",
  "comparable_wines": "Consider Domaine Gauby 2018 for similar Roussillon origin but higher price and more natural wine focus. Clos des Fées Les Sorcières offers another old vine Roussillon blend with comparable density and spice. Alvaro Palacios Priorat Camins shares the schist soil profile but offers higher acidity and lighter body.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry red with supple tannins and dark mineral drive",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Keep this bottle within five years of release to capture the fruit energy, as the concrete aging does not build long-term oxidative stability. Store upright for short term, but lay flat for anything beyond six months to keep the cork moist.",
  "value_assessment": "$30 to $40 CAD places this directly against mid-tier Priorat and high-end Languedoc blends on the shelf. Competitors like Mas Amiel or Villa Blanche often charge similar rates but rely more heavily on oak seasoning to mask fruit quality. This bottle delivers better farming transparency at this price point, making it a solid buy for weekly rotation.",
  "market_position": "You will find this wine on restaurant by-the-glass lists where customers want structure without heavy tannins. Retail buyers stock it for shoppers seeking French labeling reliability without Burgundy or Bordeaux costs. Collectors ignore it, but casual drinkers who understand warm climate profiles return to it consistently.",
  "insider_take": "Skip the standard Cotes du Roussillon and pay the extra few dollars for the Old Vines designation because the depth difference is tangible. Many assume large production equals diluted quality, but Lafage proves volume and character can coexist when farming is strict. You will not find more consistent typicity in this price bracket from the south of France.",

parsed.hook: From schist and gneiss slopes across the Roussillon, Tessellae Old Vines builds a dense, dark red with distinct mineral pressure. This cuvée exists to prove that high-volume production can still express site specificity without losing drinkability.
parsed.wine_summary: Operating at a scale few quality producers attempt, Jean-Michel Lafage bottles hundreds of thousands of cases while maintaining farming standards that respect the dry Mediterranean climate. The Tessellae label serves as the entry point to his portfolio, yet the old vine designation signals access to deeper root systems capable of surviving the region's brutal tramontane winds. Roussillon heat concentrates sugars quickly, but the old vines moderate vigor, resulting in a wine that balances ripe fruit weight with structural integrity.
parsed.terroir_expression: Black schist and gneiss dominate the best sites here, storing heat during the day and releasing it at night to ensure full phenolic ripeness even in cooler vintages. These metamorphic rocks fracture easily, forcing roots to dig deep for water, which stresses the vine and reduces yield naturally. The resulting wine carries a dark mineral edge rather than just sweet fruit, distinguishing it from blends grown on alluvial clay near the riverbeds.
parsed.vinification_summary: To preserve primary fruit character, fermentation happens in concrete vats rather than new oak, allowing oxygen exchange through the porous walls. Lafage avoids heavy extraction techniques, opting for a shorter maceration period to keep tannins supple instead of grippy. This approach utilizes partial carbonic maceration elements to enhance freshness, ensuring the wine remains vibrant despite the high alcohol potential of the region.
parsed.food_pairing: Lamb shoulder braised with anchovies works because the salt cuts the ripe fruit while the fat matches the wine's body. Nashville hot chicken finds relief in the wine's glycerol texture and low overt tannin. Grilled sardines with romesco complement the schist-driven smokiness in the finish. Mushroom risotto aligns earthy notes with the old vine depth without overwhelming the palate. Beef cheek tacos stand up to the alcohol warmth while the acid cleanses the fat.
parsed.comparable_wines: Consider Domaine Gauby 2018 for similar Roussillon origin but higher price and more natural wine focus. Clos des Fées Les Sorcières offers another old vine Roussillon blend with comparable density and spice. Alvaro Palacios Priorat Camins shares the schist soil profile but offers higher acidity and lighter body.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with supple tannins and dark mineral drive
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Keep this bottle within five years of release to capture the fruit energy, as the concrete aging does not build long-term oxidative stability. Store upright for short term, but lay flat for anything beyond six months to keep the cork moist.
parsed.value_assessment: $30 to $40 CAD places this directly against mid-tier Priorat and high-end Languedoc blends on the shelf. Competitors like Mas Amiel or Villa Blanche often charge similar rates but rely more heavily on oak seasoning to mask fruit quality. This bottle delivers better farming transparency at this price point, making it a solid buy for weekly rotation.
parsed.market_position: You will find this wine on restaurant by-the-glass lists where customers want structure without heavy tannins. Retail buyers stock it for shoppers seeking French labeling reliability without Burgundy or Bordeaux costs. Collectors ignore it, but casual drinkers who understand warm climate profiles return to it consistently.
parsed.insider_take: Skip the standard Cotes du Roussillon and pay the extra few dollars for the Old Vines designation because the depth difference is tangible. Many assume large production equals diluted quality, but Lafage proves volume and character can coexist when farming is strict. You will not find more consistent typicity in this price bracket from the south of France.
